1:
The psalm opens with no narrative occasion, only a heading — "To the chief Musician, A Psalm of David" — before it plunges into its verdict on the age, that "the fool hath said in his heart, There is no God." The witnesses agree almost to a voice that the folly here is not speculative but practical. The reformed John Gill takes the "fool," Hebrew nabal, not for a single man such as Nabal or Nebuchadnezzar but for a whole body or set of men — not idiots void of common sense but fools in morals, wicked and profane, who work themselves into the belief, or at least the wish, that there is no God; they say it in the heart, that desperately wicked seat out of which the atheism proceeds. John Calvin, the other reformed voice, presses that nabal means not the common dullard but the perverse and vile man, and that David inveighs not against the simple but against those the world accounts wise: there is, Calvin says, no stupidity more brutish than the forgetfulness of God. These men frame no syllogisms that there is no God; rather the unbridled licence of their life sings them the song in a heart from which they have laboured to efface all remembrance of his majesty.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sorts the atheism into three sorts — the few who deny God’s existence outright, those who allow a Being of infinite power yet give him no world to govern, and the many who, professing to own both, live as though there were no God to punish or reward. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears the sinner whisper his creed secretly in his heart, not as a settled judgment but as an imagination he cannot prove yet wishes true, for no man will say there is no God till it has become his interest that there should be none to call him to account; and Charles Spurgeon, the other puritan-evangelical voice, calls the atheist a fool pre-eminently, since to deny God is to belie the plainest evidence, to oppose the common consent of mankind, and to stifle conscience.

The grammatical-historical witnesses add the wider bearing. Charles Ellicott derives nabal from a root meaning "to wither," so that fool and wicked become almost synonymous, and marks that where this psalm reads "abominable works" its near-twin reads "iniquity." Keil and Delitzsch observe that in Ps. 53 this very psalm recurs in Elohimic dress, and judge the present Jehovic form the earlier and more original composition. The latin-fathers Augustine reads even the heading toward Christ, taking the "end" of the title for him to whom the believer presses; and John Wesley, briefly, glosses the "fool" as simply the wicked man and the "good" he cannot do as the actions truly pleasing to God.
2:
Against the atheist’s whisper that no eye is watching, the psalm sets the eye that searches all — "the LORD looked down from heaven upon the children of men." The reformed John Gill reads the line as a direct rejoinder to the impious reasonings of the first verse: there is a God, and though his throne is in the heavens he takes cognizance of all human affairs; the looking-down is an anthropopathy, a speaking after the manner of men, denoting the exact and accurate knowledge he has of men and their doings, consistent with his omniscience and omnipresence. John Wesley agrees that God knows all things without enquiry and speaks so only after the manner of men, and takes the "children of men" for the whole Israelitish nation and indeed all mankind, his own people and the righteous alone excepted.

The grammatical-historical witnesses fix the picture in the verb. Keil and Delitzsch note that the word means to look forth by bending oneself forward, the proper term for looking out of a window and for God’s looking down from heaven, and that "to see" recalls the history of the tower of Babel, when the LORD came down to look (Gen. 11:5); his all-piercing eyes scrutinise the whole human race. Charles Ellicott renders it likewise, "bent forward to look as from a window," and sharpens the object: better than "did understand" is "any man of understanding," set in deliberate contrast with the "fool" of the opening — one who orders his conduct on the conviction that a holy and just God exists.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke pictures God from his glorious eminence looking upon the habitable globe to see whether any understand that there is a Supreme Being, the Governor and Judge of men, and in consequence seek him. The puritan-evangelical Charles Spurgeon dwells on the justice of the search: the Lord will not punish blindly nor order an indiscriminate massacre upon a rumour, but gazes intently, as he visited Sodom before he overthrew it, searching out the righteous that they perish not with the guilty. Yet the search, Spurgeon owns, proves fruitless — of all the race of Adam no unrenewed soul is other than an enemy to God and goodness; the Lord looks only for any that understand their state and seek him, and surely, if men had any right understanding, they would seek him. The witnesses do not divide: the God whom the fool denies is the God whose eye is even now upon him.
3:
The divine survey ends in a universal indictment, and the witnesses gather at the sweep of it: "they are all gone aside, they are all together become filthy: there is none that doeth good, no, not one." The reformed John Gill hears the men gone aside as bankrupts run out of their whole stock, revolted from God and turned their backs on his commandment; the Apostle Paul, he notes, renders it "they are all gone out of the way," out of the path of righteousness into the way of sin and death. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, whose comment reaches from the first verse over this one, calls the apostasy universal — there is none that doeth good, no, not one, till the free and mighty grace of God has wrought a change — and insists that whatever good is found in any of the children of men is not of themselves but God’s work in them.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch measure the Hebrew’s force: the totality (hakol), together (yachdav), not a single one excepted; sar is to fall away, the very word for an apostate, and ne’elach paints the corruption as a turning sour, a putrefaction (Job 15:16). It is these three verses, they observe, that Paul quotes (Rom. 3:10-12) to prove from Scripture that Jew and heathen alike are shut up under sin. Charles Ellicott, the other grammatical-historical voice, glosses "filthy" as corrupt or putrid and hears in it the Roman satirist’s lament that vice had reached its zenith. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke draws the same image from the dairy — they are become sour and rancid, like milk fermented and turned worthless — and owns this the state of the whole earth’s inhabitants until grace changes the heart; John Wesley more plainly reads them gone from God and his rule, and "filthy" as loathsome and abominable to him.

Here the great textual question of the psalm breaks open, over the six verses that the ancient versions add after this one. Ellicott records that between the third and fourth verses the Alexandrian manuscript of the Septuagint, with the Vulgate and the Arabic, inserts the passage St. Paul strings together at Rom. 3:13-18 — "their throat is an open sepulchre" and the rest — which he judges a cento gathered from various psalms and Isaiah, the copyist led to the insertion by its standing next to the quotation of these very verses. Clarke lays out the same crux at length and comes down, with Jerome, on the side of interpolation: Paul did not quote the lines from this psalm but collected them from several places to show man’s corruption, and later hands, finding them in Romans, inserted them into the Greek; he notes their absence from Origen’s Hexapla and the best copies, though Jerome owned they were read in the churches of his day. So the witnesses divide over whether the added verses ever belonged to the psalm — a question that turns, as ever, on whether Paul is quoting the psalm or the psalter is quoting Paul. The latin-fathers Augustine, reading the bare "none that doeth good, no, not one," finds room in the phrase "up to one" for the Lord Christ to be excepted, since no man did good until he first showed it.
4:
The indictment turns from the many to the cruel, and the psalm rounds on the persecutors with a question of wonder — "have all the workers of iniquity no knowledge?" The reformed John Gill reads the question not as granting their ignorance but as marvelling at it, or even denying it: these are no sinners of the Gentiles feeling their way by nature’s light, but sinners in Zion, who had the revelation and law of the one God of Israel and so sinned against knowledge. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch take "not to know" absolutely, in the sense of being without sense or conscience, and hear the divine outburst aimed at the sinners in Israel, as when the Judge of the world arraigns the heads of his people (Isa. 3:13-15).

On the second clause the witnesses press the fearful image of men who "eat up my people as they eat bread." The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears an innate and inveterate enmity: it is meat and drink to persecutors to do mischief, and they devour God’s people easily, daily, and securely, without check of conscience, as Joseph’s brethren cast him into a pit and then sat down to eat bread. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke makes them an easy and unresisting prey, borrowing the spies’ word that the Canaanites were "bread for us" (Num. 14:9); John Wesley reads the eating as done with as little remorse and as much greediness as a man eats his necessary food. Charles Spurgeon heaps the figures — as pikes in a pond eat little fish, as eagles prey on smaller birds, as wolves rend the sheep, so sinners naturally persecute the followers of the Lord; and while thus preying they forswear all praying, consistently enough, for how should they hope to be heard whose hands are full of blood?

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott lingers over the exact Hebrew, "eating my people they have eaten bread; on Jehovah they have not called," and suspects from the likeness to Mic. 3:3-4 that the line was a proverbial saying, recalling Homer’s "people-devouring kings." On the last clause the witnesses agree with Wesley that the men are guilty at once of gross injustice toward men and of horrid impiety toward God, and with Henry that those who care not for God’s poor care not for God himself; the reason men run into every wickedness, Henry adds, is that they call not upon God for his grace, and what good can be expected of those who live without prayer? The witnesses do not divide: the persecutor’s cruelty and his prayerlessness spring from one root, a heart that neither knows God nor calls on him.
5:
"There were they in great fear" — the scene shifts in an instant from the persecutors’ feasting to their terror, and the witnesses catch the suddenness of it. The reformed John Gill takes the fright as proof that even these men had some knowledge of God and a consciousness of guilt they could not banish; the wicked flee when no man pursues and are chased by the sound of a shaken leaf, and he recalls that the twin psalm adds "where no fear was," that is, where no cause of fear existed — as Hobbes the atheist, Gill notes, was afraid to be alone in the dark. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the "there" not as a place but as a "then" — the moment when God’s long-suffering turns to wrath and his word smites the brutish men — and note how the doubled Hebrew, "they feared a fear," heaps intensity on the dread.

Charles Ellicott hears the same, "there they feared a fear," and finds in the local "there" a picture set before the eyes: we see the wicked in the midst of their intrigues and pleasures when the hand of God seizes them; yet he warns that the verse gives no handle by which to fasten on a particular event, the uneasy sense that the good have God on their side being always a terror to the wicked. Both grammarians mark that the twin psalm adds a clause here — "which was no fear" — a chief among the small differences between the two. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sees an allusion to the Canaanitish nations struck with terror at the sight of Israel, and reads the closing ground plainly: they feared God’s people because they knew the Almighty was among them. John Wesley agrees that God struck them with a panic fear upon the very spot where they practised their insolences, for God is on their side and their enemies have cause to tremble.

The puritan-evangelical Charles Spurgeon draws the moral that as cowards are cruel, so all cruel men are at heart cowards: the loud-mouthed, iron-handed persecutors have their appointed seasons of overthrow, and an undefinable, mysterious dread creeps over the most hardened when conscience wakes. What makes the company of godly men so irksome to them, he adds, is that they perceive God is with them; like Haman they instinctively tremble when they see God’s Mordecais, for the union between God and his people is close to a mysterious indwelling. The witnesses do not divide: the fear of the persecutor is the shadow cast by the God who dwells among the righteous.
6:
The persecutors’ scorn is now named for what it is, an assault on the one comfort of the afflicted — "ye have shamed the counsel of the poor, because the LORD is his refuge." The reformed John Gill identifies the poor as the saints, the generation of the righteous, generally the poor of this world and poor in spirit; and the "counsel" not as advice they give to others but as the counsel they receive from the Lord — to trust in him and make him their refuge, the best of counsel, at which wicked men mock and by which they would shame the saints out of their hope, though hope makes not ashamed. John Wesley fixes the ground of the contempt in the last clause: it was because the poor man lived by faith in God’s promise and providence that the wicked despised him.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch note that the verb, which elsewhere means to put a person to shame, here takes a thing for its object and so means to confound or frustrate the counsel; and they hear the psalmist himself meeting the oppressed full of joyous confidence, so that where a sixth tristich was expected the poem breaks off into a quiet distich. Charles Ellicott presses the sense further, taking the "counsel" for the sufferer’s confidence and appeal to his supreme Protector, and turning the verse into a challenge — "Would ye then make the sufferer blush for such a thought? No, for Jehovah is his refuge" — and he faults the Authorised Version for missing the force by rendering the verb in the past tense. Adam Clarke, keeping the past, reports Bishop Horsley’s proposal to repoint the word so that "the counsel of the helpless man shall put them to shame," but rejects it as unwarranted by manuscript or version: no change is needed, for the point is simply that the poor took counsel to expect help from God and wait patiently, and this counsel the proud derided.

Here the readings genuinely part. The grammatical-historical Ellicott would have the verse a present taunt met at once by faith’s answer, while the received text and the wesleyan-arminian Clarke keep it a past accusation of shame already attempted. The puritan-evangelical Charles Spurgeon feels the sting of the mockery most: notwithstanding their real cowardice the wicked put on the lion’s skin and lord it over the Lord’s poor ones, and the special butt of their jest is the believer’s confidence in his Lord — "What can your God do for you now?" Let us not be laughed out of our confidence, Spurgeon urges, but scorn their scorning and defy their jeers, for we need wait but a little and the Lord our refuge will avenge his own elect. The witnesses do not divide over the comfort beneath the taunt: the refuge the wicked deride is the very refuge that will not fail.
7:
The psalm that opened in the gloom of universal corruption closes on a cry of longing for rescue: "Oh that the salvation of Israel were come out of Zion!" The reformed John Gill hears the Messiah in the word "salvation" — the Saviour of all God’s elect, whether Jew or Gentile, who was to come out of Zion, out of Judea, from among the Jews; David, he says, was one of those kings and prophets who desired to see the days of the Messiah, and the sad depravity he has just described is what moves him to wish so vehemently for that coming. John Wesley reads the same double reach: the words immediately concern the deliverance of Israel out of the sinful state just described, but principally they design the spiritual redemption of all God’s Israel by the Messiah, the "captivity" being his captive people. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, closing his long comment, lets the prospect look past David’s day: the Redeemer is expected to come to Zion to turn away ungodliness from Jacob (Rom. 11:26) — "the world is bad; O that the Messiah would come and change its character!" — and the second coming of Christ, finally to extinguish the dominion of sin and Satan, will be the completing of this salvation. Charles Spurgeon, the other puritan-evangelical voice, makes the verse the desire of the godly in all ages, who, though Christ has come once with a sin-offering, still look for him to come a second time unto salvation.

The grammatical-historical witnesses fix the idiom and the geography. Keil and Delitzsch note that "bring back the captivity" (shuv shevut) means to turn the captivity or bring back the captives, the simple form chosen for its alliteration, and that the exiles never looked for redemption anywhere but from Zion. Charles Ellicott hears the thoughts of the exiles turning to the Holy City as the one source of deliverance, as Daniel prayed toward Jerusalem; the phrase "turn the captivity" (Ps. 126:1), he adds, came to be applied proverbially to the removal of any misfortune (Job 42:10).

Beneath the shared hope the witnesses divide over the psalm’s occasion. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke judges the whole psalm a complaint of the captives in Babylon, thinks the ascription to David improperly prefixed, and cites Calmet that the remains of Israel and Judah were rejoined after the return; of the two chief opinions — Absalom’s rebellion or the Babylonish captivity — he inclines to the latter. Henry keeps it David’s own, written when he was driven out by Absalom and comforted that God would turn again his captivity to the joy of his subjects. Keil and Delitzsch hold a middle line, hearing in this closing tristich what sounds like a liturgical addition from the time of the Exile, unless one assign the whole psalm to that period. So the question stands unresolved — whether the prayer rises from a king in flight, from an exile by the rivers of Babylon, or from a later hand that fitted an old psalm for a new sorrow. The witnesses do not divide over its end: whatever the captivity, the salvation must come out of Zion, and when it comes Jacob shall rejoice and Israel be glad. The fathers, and an old Scoto-English psalter Clarke transcribes, read that salvation of none other than Christ, in whom the wrestling of Jacob and the seeing of God in Israel are alike fulfilled.
